title: Thomas (John 20:24–29)
hookLine: he wanted to touch the wounds, and then said my Lord and my God

cards: There's a phrase for people like Thomas: pics or it didn't happen. On Easter night the risen Jesus comes to the disciples behind shut doors, and Thomas isn't there.
When the others tell him, we have seen the Lord, he doesn't believe a word.

In the Douay-Rheims he says: "Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe." Not just see. Touch.
People still call him doubting Thomas.

teach.h: LET US ALSO GO, THAT WE MAY DIE WITH HIM.
teach.b: First, who Thomas was. Earlier in John, when Jesus decides to go back into Judea, where people had just tried to stone him, it's Thomas who says: "Let us also go, that we may die with him." Not a coward.
Blunt, loyal, and he won't pretend. Eight days after Easter they're together again, the doors shut, and this time Thomas is there. Jesus stands in the middle and says, "Peace be to you."
Then he offers Thomas exactly what he asked for: put in your finger, see my hands, bring your hand, put it into my side, "and be not faithless, but believing." He doesn't scold him for asking.

teach.h: NO VERSE SAYS HE TOUCHED THEM.
teach.b: And here's the surprise: the Gospel never says Thomas touched them.

What it gives us is his answer: "My Lord, and my God." The man remembered for doubting is the one who says it. Then Jesus adds a line for everyone after: "blessed are they that have not seen, and have believed."
Christians hear themselves in that line.
Catholics hear this Gospel every year on the Sunday after Easter, and by an old custom, when the priest lifts the host at Mass, some people whisper Thomas's words: my Lord and my God.
Tradition says Thomas later carried the faith all the way to India, and Christians there still call themselves Saint Thomas Christians.
So that was the week: remember me, the Stabat Mater, tetelestai, Holy Saturday, the garden, Emmaus, and Thomas.

how: Catholics hear the story of Thomas every year on the Second Sunday of Easter, and some quietly say 'my Lord and my God' when the host is raised at Mass.

o: a brother of Jesus who led Jerusalem's church
the disciple who wrote the first Gospel
the doubter who said: my Lord and my God

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: that have not seen, and have believed

s: the Gospel says Thomas put his finger in the wounds
Jesus offers, but John never says Thomas touched. he answers: my Lord, and my God.
Thomas was known as a coward
earlier he said, let us also go, that we may die with him.
Catholics hear this Gospel every year the Sunday after Easter
on the Second Sunday of Easter, in every year of the cycle.

games.q: you're Thomas. the risen Jesus stands in front of you and invites you to touch his wounds. what do you do?
o: say, my Lord, and my God.
games.why: John never says he touched. he gives us only the answer: "My Lord, and my God."

practice: Name one thing about faith, or God, or your own life, that you're not sure about; don't hide it and don't force an answer, just hold it in the open, the way Thomas said his out loud to his friends.
If you pray, you can bring it to God as plainly as he did; in the story, Jesus didn't turn him away.

wordCard.voice: Thomas. The disciple who wanted to see and touch, and who then said: my Lord and my God. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek form of an Aramaic name meaning twin. John also calls him Didymus, the Greek for twin.

carryVoice: Your line: doubt can kneel too. Honest questions have a place. Seventy days, ten weeks.
